h1: The 8 Best Ultrawide Monitors Under $500 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 ultrawide monitors under $500, all 3440x1440, compared on refresh rate, USB-C, curve and stand for work and gaming.
summary: The Dell S3425DW is the most balanced 34-inch ultrawide here: USB-C with 65W power, strong color coverage and a fast panel. The LG 34WR55QK-B is the pick if your day is spreadsheets and documents. For gaming first, the AOC CU34G4V and MSI MAG 346CQ pair 180Hz with fast response. The SANSUI 34-inch is the cheapest way into 3440x1440 at 200Hz.
intro: Every monitor on this list uses a 34-inch curved VA panel at 3440x1440. That shared resolution makes the choice simpler than it looks, because the real differences are elsewhere: whether one USB-C cable charges your laptop, how fast the panel refreshes, how tight the curve is and whether the stand lets you adjust height.

We compared the spec sheets for eight ultrawides priced under $500 and ranked them by how many buyers each would suit well. Productivity features count heavily, because most people use an ultrawide for work first. Gaming-first picks sit lower, though several of them are excellent at it.

products.name: Dell 34 Plus USB-C Curved Monitor (S3425DW)
products.verdict: USB-C with 65W power, 95% DCI-P3 color and a fast panel make it the best all-rounder.
products.description:
Dell's S3425DW is a 34-inch 3440x1440 curved VA monitor with a refresh rate up to 120Hz and a listed 0.03ms response time. It covers 99% of sRGB and 95% of DCI-P3, and a USB-C port delivers 65W of power to a laptop.

That mix is why it leads. Several others here beat its 120Hz ceiling, but none pairs the same color coverage with single-cable laptop docking. It is also covered by Dell's Premium Panel warranty. The cost is a lower refresh rate than the 180Hz gaming panels.

It suits a hybrid worker who wants a laptop on one cable, accurate color for photos and some gaming in the evening.
products.skipIf: You want the highest refresh rate.

products.name: LG 34WR55QK-B
products.verdict: USB-C 65W, Reader Mode and picture-by-picture make it a desk-work specialist.
products.description:
LG built this 34-inch ultrawide for work. It has 3440x1440 resolution, USB-C with 65W Power Delivery, a Reader Mode for long documents, picture-by-picture to show two sources, and OnScreen Control software to snap windows into zones. The stand adjusts for height and tilt.

It ranks just behind Dell because its 100Hz refresh rate is the lowest in the group, and it makes no pretense of being a gaming display. If you spend the day in spreadsheets, a code editor or video calls, that is not a flaw. It is a choice.

Best for office-first buyers who want one cable to a laptop and tools for splitting the screen.

products.name: AOC CU34G4V
products.verdict: 180Hz, 0.5ms MPRT and a stand that raises 130mm, at a price well under $300.
products.description:
AOC pairs a 34-inch 3440x1440 VA panel on a 1500R curve with a 180Hz refresh rate and a 0.5ms MPRT response. FreeSync Premium is supported, and the stand adjusts for height, swivel and tilt through a 130mm range.

The adjustable stand is rare at this price and is the reason it ranks above the MSI and Alienware for desk comfort. It has no USB-C, so a laptop needs its own charger. Against the Dell, you trade docking for a higher refresh rate and a lower cost.

A smart pick for a gamer who wants speed and ergonomics without a premium bill.
products.idealFor: Gamers who want an adjustable stand.
products.skipIf: You dock a laptop with USB-C.

products.name: MSI MAG 346CQ
products.verdict: Certified for G-Sync Compatible and FreeSync, with 180Hz, 3000:1 contrast and a height stand.
products.description:
MSI's MAG 346CQ is a 3440x1440 VA monitor at 180Hz with a 1ms MPRT, 3000:1 contrast ratio and built-in speakers. It is certified as G-Sync Compatible and FreeSync, so it fits either graphics card brand, and the stand adjusts for height.

It ranks below the AOC because the AOC lists a faster response and costs less. Where the MSI wins is the dual certification and deeper contrast. If you might switch GPU brands, that coverage is worth it.

Suits a gamer who wants a monitor to last through a graphics card swap.
products.idealFor: Gamers who may switch GPU brands.
products.skipIf: You want a USB-C laptop dock.

products.name: Alienware AW3425DWM
products.verdict: 180Hz, 1ms response and a console mode, backed by a 3-year warranty.
products.description:
Alienware's AW3425DWM combines a 34-inch 3440x1440 VA panel on a 1500R curve, 180Hz refresh, 1ms response and a 3000:1 contrast ratio. It is the only monitor here with a dedicated console mode, and it carries a 3-year warranty.

The console mode tunes the display for a PlayStation or Xbox, which makes it the better pick for a living-room desk. It ranks fifth because the spec sheet is close to the MSI's, and the MSI adds G-Sync certification and a height stand.

Best for players who split time between PC and console.
cons: Costs more than rivals with similar specs
products.idealFor: Players who use PC and console.

products.name: ASUS TUF Gaming VG34VQ3B
products.verdict: Four USB 3.2 ports, built-in speakers and a 3-year warranty on a 180Hz panel.
products.description:
ASUS packs a 34-inch 3440x1440 VA panel at 180Hz with 90% DCI-P3 coverage into the TUF Gaming VG34VQ3B. Four USB 3.2 ports act as a hub for a keyboard, mouse and drives, and built-in speakers cover casual audio. A 3-year warranty is included.

The USB hub is why it is useful on a work desk too, even without USB-C. It ranks below the MSI because the MSI offers G-Sync certification and a height stand. Against the Dell, you get more ports but no single-cable docking.

A fit for a desk with many peripherals and no laptop to charge.
products.skipIf: You dock a laptop over USB-C.

products.name: Samsung 34" Odyssey G5
products.verdict: The tightest curve here, at 1000R, with 165Hz, HDR10 and FreeSync Premium.
products.description:
Samsung's Odyssey G5 uses a 34-inch 3440x1440 VA panel on a tight 1000R curve, the most aggressive in this ranking. Refresh is 165Hz, with HDR10 support and FreeSync Premium.

The 1000R curve wraps around your field of view, which makes games feel immersive but can distort straight lines in spreadsheets or design work. It ranks below the 180Hz models for its lower refresh rate, and it lacks USB-C.

Best for gamers who want an enveloping curve and are less concerned about office work.
products.skipIf: You do design or spreadsheet work.

products.name: SANSUI 34" Curved UWQHD Monitor
products.verdict: The least expensive way into 3440x1440, with 200Hz, 97% DCI-P3 and HDMI 2.1 ports.
products.description:
SANSUI offers the lowest price in this group for a 34-inch 3440x1440 VA panel that refreshes at 200Hz. It covers 97% of DCI-P3, supports picture-in-picture and picture-by-picture, and has two HDMI 2.1 ports plus DisplayPort 1.4.

The spec sheet is impressive for the cost, which is the reason to consider it. It ranks last because lesser-known brands carry more risk on warranty and support, and it lacks USB-C and a height-adjustable stand listed in the data we have.

A reasonable choice when budget is the main limit and you can accept brand risk.
products.idealFor: Tight budgets with a PC to feed it.

methodology.title: Productivity features
methodology.description: USB-C power delivery, picture-by-picture and reading modes carried weight, since most ultrawides are used for work first.

methodology.title: Refresh and response
methodology.description: Refresh rate and listed response time were scored against what a 34-inch VA panel can deliver in games.

methodology.title: Color coverage
methodology.description: sRGB and DCI-P3 figures show which monitors suit photo and video work as well as gaming.

methodology.title: Stand and ergonomics
methodology.description: Height adjustment matters on a wide screen, so stand range counted toward each ranking.

methodology.title: Value within the field
methodology.description: Features and warranty were compared against price bracket relative to the others here.

whatMatters.detail: A USB-C port with 65W Power Delivery carries video and charges a laptop through one cable. It is only worth paying for if you use a laptop. Without it you need a separate charger and video cable. Check the wattage on the listing, since lower numbers will not charge a larger laptop.

whatMatters.factor: Curve radius is a comfort choice
whatMatters.detail: A 1000R curve is tighter than 1500R, so the screen wraps more around you. Tighter feels more immersive in games but can bend straight lines in documents. Most work-focused buyers are happier with 1500R or gentler curves.

Going from 60Hz to 100Hz or 120Hz is obvious. From 120Hz to 180Hz, the difference is smaller and mostly matters for fast shooters. Check that your graphics card can drive 3440x1440 at those rates before you pay for them.

whatMatters.factor: VA panels trade angle for contrast
whatMatters.detail: All eight monitors use VA panels, which have deeper blacks and higher contrast ratios than IPS but narrower viewing angles. Sit directly in front of the middle of the screen and the sides stay readable. Do not plan on a very close seat.

whatMatters.factor: Stand height matters on a wide screen
whatMatters.detail: A 34-inch ultrawide is tall as well as wide, so a fixed low stand can leave the top edge too high or too low. Look for a listed height range such as 130mm. If the stand is fixed, check that you can fit a VESA arm instead.

howToChoose.intro: Decide what the monitor will do most.

cards.label: USB-C docking
cards.text: One cable carries video and 65W to a laptop. Picks: Dell S3425DW and LG 34WR55QK-B.

cards.label: Gaming speed
cards.text: Higher refresh and faster response, but no laptop charging. Picks: AOC CU34G4V, MSI MAG 346CQ, Alienware AW3425DWM, ASUS TUF VG34VQ3B, SANSUI.

howToChoose.note: Choose USB-C if you use a laptop daily. Choose speed if your PC does the work.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Enough USB ports for a keyboard, mouse and drives, and a stand that does not eat desk depth.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ASUS TUF VG34VQ3B, which lists four USB 3.2 ports and built-in speakers to cut desk clutter.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You use a laptop daily or edit photos. The Dell S3425DW's USB-C and color coverage justify the premium.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You game on a desktop PC. The AOC CU34G4V or SANSUI already deliver 180Hz or more.

faq.q: Is 3440x1440 good enough, or do I need 4K ultrawide?
faq.a: For a 34-inch screen, 3440x1440 is a sharp, practical resolution and far easier on a graphics card than 4K. All eight monitors here use it.

faq.q: Do I need a USB-C monitor?
faq.a: Only if you use a laptop. The Dell S3425DW and LG 34WR55QK-B offer 65W power and video over one cable. For a desktop PC, USB-C adds little.

faq.q: Is a curved ultrawide good for work?
faq.a: Yes, especially at 1500R or gentler. The curve keeps the edges within view. The Samsung's tighter 1000R curve is better suited to games than documents.

faq.q: What refresh rate do I need?
faq.a: For office work, 100Hz is plenty. For gaming, 144Hz to 180Hz feels very smooth. Check that your graphics card can drive 3440x1440 at that rate.
Many consoles do not output true 21:9, so they show black bars. The Alienware AW3425DWM has a console mode designed for this case.

faq.q: Can I mount these on a monitor arm?
faq.a: Many monitors support VESA mounts, but ultrawides are heavy and wide. Check the listing for VESA support and the weight limit of your arm before you buy.

finalTake: For most buyers the Dell S3425DW is the best ultrawide under $500: USB-C with 65W power, strong color and a fast panel. If work is the whole story, the LG 34WR55QK-B has the tools for it. Gamers should look at the AOC CU34G4V for value or the MSI MAG 346CQ for dual sync certification. On a tight budget, the SANSUI 34-inch gets you 3440x1440 at 200Hz for the least.
